1151 * The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the city of Śrāvastī and announce to the fourfold assembly: ‘Friends, tomorrow the Blessed One will perform the second great miracle of the Tathāgata at the gate of the city of Śrāvastī. “Very well, Lord,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having received his instruction, he went to the city of Śrāvastī and announced to the fourfold assembly: “Friends, tomorrow the Blessed One will perform the second great miracle of the Tathāgata at the gate of the city of Śrāvastī. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished his almsround in the city of Śrāvastī, he returned from the almsround, ate his meal, and set out for the gate of the city of Śrāvastī. There he washed his feet, entered the gate of the city of Śrāvastī, and stood upon the threshold. At that time, the Blessed One performed the second great miracle of the Tathāgata. From the gate of the city of Śrāvastī, he rose up into the air to the height of seven palm trees; from the height of seven palm trees, he rose up to the height of eight; from the height of eight, he rose up to the height of nine; from the height of nine, he rose up to the height of ten; from the height of ten, he rose up to the height of eleven; from the height of eleven, he rose up to the height of twelve; from the height of twelve, he rose up to the height of thirteen; Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as 'Buddha'? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even a minute particle of a dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as 'Buddha. Therefore, Blessed One, the Tathāgata speaks of 'the perfection of wisdom' as being 'perfection of wisdom,' because it is without any basis for apprehension. Furthermore, Blessed One, if someone were to fill this billion-fold world system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and if another person were to take up even so much as a single four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others, the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit than the former. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have fully awakened to all dharmas through this very perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Blessed One, one should know that this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the nurse of the Bodhisattvas, and the progenitor of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should practice it in such a way that he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor the Bodhisattva, nor the one who practices, nor the practice itself.

Why is that? Because, Blessed One, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. They are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor purified. This is called the 'perfection of wisdom' of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. [End of Chapter 217]

*** 008 •• The Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones. The Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. Right View is to understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Right Resolve is to renounce worldly desires, to harbor no ill will, and to maintain right views. Right Speech is to abstain from lying, divisive speech, harsh words, and idle chatter. Right Action is to abstain from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Right Livelihood is to earn one's living by means that do not involve the five kinds of wrong livelihood. Right Effort is to exert oneself to prevent unwholesome states from arising, to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen, to cultivate wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and to increase wholesome states that have already arisen. Right Mindfulness is to dwell with clear comprehension and mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena. Right Concentration is to attain the four jhānas through detachment, dispassion, and cessation, having abandoned sensual desire and unwholesome states. *** 009 •• The Ninefold Path of the Noble Ones. The Ninefold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, and Right Knowledge. Right Knowledge is to know as it truly is: "This is suffering," "This is the origin of suffering," "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. *** 010 •• The Tenfold Path of the Noble Ones. The Tenfold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right Knowledge, and Right Liberation. Right Liberation is to be liberated from all defilements through the destruction of craving, the fading away of greed, and the cessation of ignorance. *** 011 •• The Elevenfold Path of the Noble Ones. The Elevenfold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right Knowledge, Right Liberation, and Right Abandonment. Right Abandonment is to abandon the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. *** 012 •• The Twelvefold Path of the Noble Ones. The Twelvefold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right Knowledge, Right Liberation, Right Abandonment, and Right Fulfillment. Right Fulfillment is to fulfill the practice of the Dhamma by attaining the fruit of Arhatship. *** 013 •• The Thirteenfold Path of the Noble Ones. The Thirteenfold Path of the Noble Ones consists of: Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right Knowledge, Right Liberation, Right Abandonment, Right Fulfillment, and Right Deliverance. Right Deliverance is to be delivered from the cycle of birth and death, reaching the state of Nibbāna. *** 014 •• The Four Foundations of Mindfulness. The Four Foundations of Mindfulness are: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of mental phenomena. *** 015 •• The Four Right Strivings. The Four Right Strivings are: the striving to prevent unwholesome states from arising, the striving to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen, the striving to cultivate wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and the striving to increase wholesome states that have already arisen. *** 016 •• The Four Bases of Psychic Power. The Four Bases of Psychic Power are: concentration based on the desire-to-act, concentration based on energy, concentration based on the mind, and concentration based on investigation. *** 017 •• The Five Faculties. The Five Faculties are: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. *** 018 •• The Five Powers. The Five Powers are: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. *** 019 •• The Seven Factors of Enlightenment. The Seven Factors of Enlightenment are: mindfulness, investigation of the Dhamma, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. *** 020 •• The Eight Liberations. The Eight Liberations are: possessing form, one sees forms; not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally; being intent on the beautiful; the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling. *** 021 •• The Nine Progressive Abidings. The Nine Progressive Abidings are: the abiding of the first jhāna, the abiding of the second jhāna, the abiding of the third jhāna, the abiding of the fourth jhāna, the abiding of the sphere of infinite space, the abiding of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the abiding of the sphere of nothingness, the abiding of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the abiding of the cessation of perception and feeling. *** 022 •• The Ten Totalities. The Ten Totalities are: the totality of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness. *** 023 •• The Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths are: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. *** 024 •• The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment. The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are: the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, the Four Right Strivings, the Four Bases of Psychic Power, the Five Faculties, the Five Powers, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, and the Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones. *** 025 •• The Four Analytical Knowledges. The Four Analytical Knowledges are: analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of eloquence. *** 026 •• The Four Discriminations. The Four Discriminations are: discrimination of meaning, discrimination of phenomena, discrimination of language, and discrimination of eloquence.

*** 027 •• The Four Unobstructed Knowledges. The Four Unobstructed Knowledges are: unobstructed knowledge of meaning, unobstructed knowledge of phenomena, unobstructed knowledge of language, and unobstructed knowledge of eloquence. *** 028 •• The Four Analytical Insights. The Four Analytical Insights are: insight into the past, insight into the future, insight into the present, and insight into the exhaustion of the outflows. *** 029 •• The Four Kinds of Confidence. The Four Kinds of Confidence are: confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Sangha, and confidence in the training. *** 030 •• The Four Fearlessnesses. The Four Fearlessnesses are: fearlessness in claiming perfect enlightenment, fearlessness in declaring the destruction of the outflows, fearlessness in proclaiming the obstacles to the path, and fearlessness in teaching the way to the cessation of suffering. *** 031 •• The Four Kinds of Self-Mastery. The Four Kinds of Self-Mastery are: mastery over the mind, mastery over the body, mastery over the faculties, and mastery over the elements. *** 032 •• The Four Kinds of Perfect Assurance. The Four Kinds of Perfect Assurance are: assurance regarding the past, assurance regarding the future, assurance regarding the present, and assurance regarding the exhaustion of the outflows. *** 033 •• The Four Kinds of Great Compassion. The Four Kinds of Great Compassion are: compassion for those who suffer, compassion for those who are afflicted, compassion for those who are deluded, and compassion for those who are destitute. *** 034 •• The Four Kinds of Unsurpassed Qualities. The Four Kinds of Unsurpassed Qualities are: unsurpassed virtue, unsurpassed concentration, unsurpassed wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation. ***

[Fragmentary Text] ...the venerable one said: "Venerable sirs, this is the Dharma-vinaya; this is the Teacher's instruction. Let us dwell together in concord, without dispute, with a single mind, like milk and water, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, the benefit, and the happiness of gods and humans. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the monks: "Venerable sirs, let us go to Śrāvastī to see the Blessed One, to pay our respects, and to hear the Dharma. The monks replied: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is well; let us go. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with a great assembly of monks, set out for Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages, they arrived at Śrāvastī. There, the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the community of monks has been divided. Venerable sirs have said: 'This is the Dharma-vinaya; this is the Teacher's instruction. Let us dwell together in concord, without dispute, with a single mind, like milk and water, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, the benefit, and the happiness of gods and humans.

Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for the division of the community of monks? The Blessed One said: "Mahākāśyapa, there are four causes for the division of the community of monks. What are the four? Here, Mahākāśyapa, a monk who is not himself learned teaches the Dharma to others without having mastered it; he speaks of what he has not seen as if he had seen it, and of what he has not heard, not sensed, and not known as if he had heard, sensed, and known it. This, Mahākāśyapa, is the first cause for the division of the community of monks. Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa, a monk who is himself learned teaches the Dharma to others after having mastered it; he speaks of what he has seen as if he had seen it, and of what he has heard, sensed, and known as if he had heard, sensed, and known it. However, he teaches the Dharma to others with a mind of malice, seeking to create discord. This, Mahākāśyapa, is the second cause for the division of the community of monks. Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa, a monk who is himself learned teaches the Dharma to others after having mastered it; he speaks of what he has seen as if he had seen it, and of what he has heard, sensed, and known as if he had heard, sensed, and known it. He does not teach the Dharma to others with a mind of malice, nor does he seek to create discord; however, he teaches the Dharma to others while being attached to gain, honor, and fame. This, Mahākāśyapa, is the third cause for the division of the community of monks. Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa, a monk who is himself learned teaches the Dharma to others after having mastered it; he speaks of what he has seen as if he had seen it, and of what he has heard, sensed, and known as if he had heard, sensed, and known it. He does not teach the Dharma to others with a mind of malice, nor does he seek to create discord, nor is he attached to gain, honor, and fame; however, he teaches the Dharma to others while being possessed by pride and conceit. This, Mahākāśyapa, is the fourth cause for the division of the community of monks. These, Mahākāśyapa, are the four causes for the division of the community of monks. [End of Fragment]

The Mountain of Love.
O protector of the earth, the great gift should always be given, for it yields great fruit;
especially during the dark fortnight, and even more so on that particular occasion.
The new moon day and the twelfth lunar day are declared to yield great fruit;
specifically, that which occurs in the dark fortnight after the month of Āśvayuja has passed.
O King, on the new moon day— which is greatly meritorious— and especially on the twelfth day,
a lamp filled with oil should be offered at the right side of the Lord. O King, one should prepare a wick there using eight palas of cotton.
But with a garment entirely dyed with mahārajana.
O King, a tulā of ghee should be offered on the left side of the deity;
one should also cause a meritorious, white wick, measuring eight palas, to be presented.
Wearing a complete garment, fasting, and with senses subdued,
O Lord of the Earth, one should endure this conduct in such a manner.
Having enjoyed [the fruits of merit] for a long time in the heavenly world, when he is born again upon the earth,
he becomes endowed with fortune, beauty, and good luck.
O tiger among kings, in that kingdom, in that country, and likewise in that city and family, his radiance was born like that of the sun.
He becomes victorious in battles and in quarrels;
he is exceedingly exalted.
The virtues of the virtuous always attain renown in the world.
Or, by deceiving one of these two, he obtains whatever is desired; O sinless one, he attains everything in the human state that has been described by me to you.
O King, the gift of even an ordinary lamp yields great fruit;
how much more so for a magnificent one—for its fruit has no end.
The gift of a lamp is certainly a source of great merit for any deity whatsoever.
Cemādri:
[Vrata-khaṇḍa, Chapter 1]
How much more so, then, for the God of gods, the infinite, the Great-Souled One?
It should be given on mountain peaks, on the sandy banks of rivers,
at crossroads, in forests, and in the houses of Brahmins.
O Great Mantra, the gift of lamps in high places, at the bases of trees, in cow-pens, and in dense forests, brings about great fruit.
Thus ends the procedure regarding major transgressions.
Now, the time for commencing a vow.
Regarding this, Satyavrata says:
If a lunar day (tithi) should not fall in the middle of the day due to its rising time, it is "khaṇḍā" (defective);
it is unfit for the commencement or completion of religious observances (vratas).
Regarding the commencement of the *akhanda* (unbroken) *mārttaṇḍa* that exceeds this [duration], Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"If the lunar day (*tithi*) should be unbroken, pervading two solar days (*khakhavyāpin*)."
The commencement of her vow should take place when Jupiter and Venus have not set.

The meaning is that if a lunar day (tithi) is joined with Jupiter and Venus that have not set—that is, joined with Jupiter and Venus that have not gone to their setting—then the commencement of the vow (vrata) should be undertaken on that day. This is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that the commencement of the vow may be undertaken even when Jupiter and Venus are in any other position [such as retrograde or stationary].
And so it is stated in the Manu-smṛti:
"The establishment of the sacred fires, the performance of sacrifices, giving gifts, and the observance of vows..."
One should avoid in the intercalary month (malamāsa) the Vedic vows, the shaving of the beard, the tonsure ceremony, the girdle-tying rite, auspicious ceremonies, and royal consecrations.
Or perhaps joy; what indeed is in the Guru?
[Chapter 1 of the Vrata-khaṇḍa, page 282]
Hemādri states: "One should avoid these [rites] during an intercalary month, as well as the viewing of the deity."

The naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the marriage, the investiture with the sacred girdle, the rite of going out [from the house], the birth-rite, and the optional release of a bull.
When Jupiter or Indra (Jupiter) has set, when the moon is in its infancy or old age, or during the intercalary month,
one should by no means perform the commencement or the conclusion of religious vows.
If [the Moon] is situated in the seventh house, retrograde, in a state of transgression, or set in the house of children,
then renunciation, pilgrimage to sacred sites, the performance of vows, ear-piercing, and initiation [are forbidden].

O Preceptor of the Lord of the Thirty-three, when the Sun is situated in the sign of Leo, one should diligently perform the Mauñjī-bandha, the Cūḍā ceremony, the marriage rite, the consecration of deities in a dwelling, and the Vardhāpana.
Regarding the characteristics of the *nīca* (depressed) sign, it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"In the case of the Sun and other planets, Aries and the following signs up to Capricorn are *nīca* in order;
furthermore, Virgo, Libra, and Gemini are also *nīca*."
The meaning is that the seventh position from the exalted station (uccasthāna) is the debased (nīca). Thus, when Jupiter is in its debased position means when it is situated in Capricorn (makara).

Śaunaka says: [The rites include] fame, building a house, marriage, sacrifice, travel, shaving the head and so forth, piercing the ears, learning, beholding the gods, initiation (*upanayana*), consecration (*dīkṣā*), examination, and religious observance (*vrata*).
Bathing, visiting sacred fords, battle, great gifts, consecration,
and the attainment of yoga— this is the reading in the *Pustakāmāra*.

24.6 Premādri, Vṛttakhaṇḍa 1, Chapter 1: When [the Moon] is in Leo, it is not auspicious for the performer [of the rite], even if it is honored by the wise; likewise when it is in the sign of the Sun.
Regarding the eight characteristics, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"The conjunction of the other planets with the sun is called 'setting' (*asta*);
one should know that which is below [the horizon] as the indicator (*vācaka*), and that which is above as the statement (*vākya*) is proclaimed."
The limit for these two has been shown in various ways in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*):
Śakra is a child for ten days and an old man for five;
thereafter, he is declared to be neither [child nor old] for three days in sequence.
A living being is always considered an infant by others even when aged, while an infant is said by some to be ten days old and by others seven nights old.
The application of these five [periods] pertains either to other regions or to times of distress.
Thus says Gārgya:
"Jupiter is Śakra when it is in the eastern or western half of its course."
"Throughout all the ten directions, for seven nights;
in these and those [places], and in the remaining regions as well, they say [it is] even for a day."
Varāhamihira also says:
"Many times have been shown for both childhood and old age;
among those, the greater ones should be adopted, while the remaining are due to differences in location or other circumstances."

Now, the characteristics of the mudrās: Having brought the two hands together with the fingers slightly contracted, it is called the *sukula*; that same [gesture] with the hands extended is the *paṅkaja*.
Vrata-khaṇḍa, Chapter 1:
Hemādri.
The Mudrās of the Closed Bud:
As before, it is the closed bud, with the fingers extended at the tip.
One should display the blooming mudrā, the bud mudrā, and the lotus mudrā.
Regarding the lotus mudrā: having joined both hands facing each other, one should clench them firmly while wrapping one's own fingers around [the other]. Niṣṭhurā.
In the *niṣṭhurā* [mudrā],
the index fingers are bent inward, and likewise the little fingers;
with the palms facing downward and the nails visible, they rest in the middle of the hand.
Raise four fingers on the back and bend them slightly like a thumb;
when two are positioned as a stalk, this is proclaimed as the Vyoma-mudrā.
[This concludes] the Vyomamudrā.
Now, regarding the seers (*ṛṣi*), deities (*daivata*), and meters (*chandas*) of the Vedic mantras,
Yājñavalkya states their purpose as follows:
The sage, the meter, the deity, and likewise the ritual application—
these must be known with diligent effort, especially by a Brahmin.

But he who performs officiating at sacrifices, teaching, recitation, silent prayer, oblation within the water, or giving of gifts without knowing [the rules], shall obtain only meager fruit for those acts.
Likewise:
"He who understands the seer, the meter, the deity,
the application, the Brāhmaṇa, the meaning of the mantra, and the ritual action of the mantras..."

Even for each individual sage, he shall be like a guest who brings no fruit;
yet there is no doubt that he attains union with the deity here.
The twice-born who knows the sages and other [details] in the manner previously described shall possess the authority to perform the secret rites and others.
That by which a seer saw [the truth], that by which he attained accomplishment,
and whatever was spoken by him through his mantra— such is the state of being of the seer, known as the *ārṣaka* (seer-originated).
Just as a form is concealed by a garment, so too was the Self (Ātman) formerly covered by the gods out of fear of death; thus, desire is designated from the act of desiring.
Āditya is thus [the deity] of the *sabhī* [meter], and Rudra is the deity of those *chandāṃsi*.
Whichever deity is specified for whichever mantra, that mantra takes on the form of that deity; its divinity is said to be the deity itself.
In ancient times, the mantras and their purposes were brought forth by the gods;
that which must be performed with this [mantra] is called its application (viniyoga).
The etymological explanation of the mantra, its application and purpose,
its foundation, and its praise— this is what is here called the Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, one should recollect this fivefold yoga at the time of recitation (japa), as well as during fire-offerings (homa), while submerged in water, in meditative union (yoga), in private study (svādhyāya), and likewise in officiating at sacrifices (yājana).

Therein, first are the mantras of the Ṛgveda. For the hymn beginning with "agnimīle," Madhukanda Viśvāmitra is the seer, Agni is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the seven verses beginning with "vāyavāyāhi," Madhukanda is the seer.
For the first three [verses], the deity is Vāyu; for the next three, Indra and Vāyu;
for the seventh, Mitra and Varuṇa. For all seven, the meter is Gāyatrī.
Chapter 1: On the Observance of Vows.
[Cemādri:
For the mantra *sahasampatim*, the seer is Medhātithi Kāṇva, the deity is Sahasampati, and the meter is Gāyatrī.
For *ambayo yanty abhi* and *tyam abhi*, the seer is Medhātithi Kāṇva, the deity is Āpaḥ, and the meter is Gāyatrī.
For *sisāsasi somapāḥ*, the seer is Śunaḥśepha Prājogata, and the deity is Indra.
The *paṅkti* meter for the seven *pāyasas*; the *gāyatrī* for the nine [verses] beginning with "yuvānā.
Medhātithi Kāṇva is the seer of "yuvānā," the *Ṛbhus* are the deities, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter.
Medhātithi Kāvya is the seer of "syonā pṛthivī," Pṛthivī is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter.
For the two verses beginning with *pratodena*, Medhātithi Deva is the seer, Viṣṇu is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter.
For the hymn of fifteen verses beginning with *kasya nūnam*, either Ājogarti Vāmadeva or Śunaḥśepha is the seer; for the first verse, Prajāpati is the deity and Triṣṭubh is the meter.
In the second [verse], Agni is the deity and Triṣṭubh is the meter.
In the three verses beginning with "abhivṛta," Savitṛ is the deity.
In this verse beginning with "bhagasya," Bhaga is the deity and Gāyatrī is the meter.
The ten verses beginning with "mahita" are Vāruṇī Triṣṭubhs.
For the eighteenth [hymn], "tvam agne prathamo 'ṅgirāḥ," the seer is Hiraṇyastūpa Aṅgirasa and the deity is Agni; the meter is Jagatī.
The eight verses beginning with "ṣoḍaśī" and the eight beginning with "aṣṭādi" are *triṣṭubh*s.
"Etā" and the five following are by Aṅgiras Prāṅkṣa; "hiraṇyastūpa" is an *indra-triṣṭubh*.
"kadudro" and the nine following are by Ghora Kāṇva; they are addressed to Rudra.
In the *atyā* verse, Rudra is the deity; in the three verses beginning with the seventh, Soma is the deity; the meter is *gāyatrī*.
The other verse, "yāste," is *anuṣṭubh*.
Hemādri:
[Vrata-khaṇḍa, Chapter 1] "ud u tyam jātavedasam" (RV 1.50.1)—these three verses; the meter is Triṣṭubh; the seer is Praskanva.
Sūrya: [The first] verse is in Pādyā; there are nine Gāyatrīs. The four verses beginning with the tenth are Anuṣṭubhs; the others are in Rogana.
Ayodhyārtha is Śatrughna. These are the meters of the ten-verse hymn.
The *pārāśara* [verse] is the *agnirhi* [meter], the *dvipadā virāj*;
according to the opinion of Śaunaka, it is the *pati virāj*.
The *rapirna vicādam artham ātayaḥ* [verse] is the *pārāśara*, the *agnirhi*, the *dvipadā virāj*.
In the opinion of Śaunaka, there are five *pachakti*s; [the hymn] beginning with *vaneṣu jāyuḥ* has ten according to Gonaka, five according to Śaunaka;

[the hymn] beginning with *śroṇām* has ten according to Śaunaka, five according to [others]; [the hymn] beginning with *vaneṣu apūrvī* has eleven according to Mīnaka, six according to [others]; [the hymns] beginning with *upaprajinvan* and *damayasya* are *śāktya*s of Pārāśarya.
The *Ṛṣi* is Romitra; the *Chandas* is Triṣṭubh; the *Devatā* is Nikāya-vedhas. For the ten verses, the *Ṛṣi* is Parāśara; the *Devatā* is Agni; the *Chandas* is Triṣṭubh.
For the group of ten verses beginning with "rarniyaḥ," the *Ṛṣi* is Pitṛvitta.
*Parāśara*, *agni*, and *triṣṭubh*;
*upaprayantaḥ*, nine verses, *rāhūgaṇa*, *gautama*, *agni*, and *gāyatrī*;
*hiraṇyakeśī*, *rajasaḥ*, *dādarthasya*, *gautama*, *agni*, and the first three [verses].

[The next] three are *triṣṭubh*s. Among them, Agni is either the one situated in the middle or the ball (*guḍa*). The [next] three, beginning with the fourth, are *uṣṇih*s. After that, there are six *gāyatrī*s.
"O Soma, you are the great illuminator; do not neglect us"—this hymn of twenty-three verses belongs to Gautama.
Regarding the first four verses, Soma is the seer and the meter is *triṣṭubh*; for the following twelve verses, the meter is *gāyatrī*.
The seventh [verse] is uṣṇih; thereafter, the sixth is triṣṭubh.
Vrata 1, Chapter: Hemādri; [verse] 251; for Prapandin, eleven verses; Āṅgirasa Kutsa; Mahatvān Indra.

The seven verses beginning with *cāyāḥ* are in the *jagatī* meter; they are the Upaniṣad for one who causes miscarriage. Following that are four verses in the *triṣṭubh* meter, beginning with *imā rudrāya tapase*, which constitute the eleventh [section].
*Kumo rudraḥ* (The Cloud as Rudra) consists of nine verses in the *jagatī* meter;
the tenth and eleventh are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The hymn beginning with *ubhe punāmahe* consists of seven verses. *Pāracepa* is addressed to Indra, and its meter is *viṣṭap*.

In this [hymn], there are three *anuṣṭubh*s; the fifth is a *gāyatrī*, the sixth is a *dhṛti*, and the seventh is a *uṣṇih*. "O gods" (*yed devāsaḥ*) is addressed to Pārucepa; the [verse] "Viśve devāḥ" is a *triṣṭubh*.
The father’s hymn consists of eleven verses. The first is an *anuṣṭubh*; the second is a *garbhoṣṇik*; the third and fourth are *gāyatrīs*; the third [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh*;
the three beginning with the fifth are *anuṣṭubhs*; then three *gāyatrīs*; and finally an *antarā bṛhatī* and an *anuṣṭubh*.

"ambena yety aṣṭau. Agastya is the seer, Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. "bhagaṃ dhiyaṃ vṛṣabham" is a group of eight verses; Bhagastya is the seer, Bṛhaspati is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter.
He recites fifteen verses beginning with *upa sṛja*. Gṛtsamada is the seer; Aponaptr is the deity; the metre is Triṣṭubh.
"Karikradad..."—Gṛtsamada is the seer, Śakuntala is the deity, Indra is the deity, and the metre is Triṣṭubh.
"Parvatā... consists of twenty-four verses; in the first [verse], Indra and Parvata are the deities. Then...
Indra is the deity for those [verses] ending with the fourteenth;
then for two [verses], Sasarparī-vāk; for the four beginning with the seventeenth, the chariot-parts;
and for the four ending with Indra, Indra is the deity.
The reading "nakṣo 'yam" is found in the Pulakāra manuscript.
Hemādri:
[Vrata, Chapter 1] The first nine are Triṣṭubh verses; the tenth and eleventh are Jagatī verses; the eleventh is a Triṣṭubh.

The twelfth is an *anuṣṭubh*; the thirteenth is a *gāyatrī*; then the fourteenth is a *triṣṭubh* and the fifteenth is a *jagatī*; the sixteenth is a *triṣṭubh*; the eighteenth is a *kaṭī*; the nineteenth is a *triṣṭubh*;
the twentieth and thirty-second are *anuṣṭubhs*; and the twenty-first and twenty-third [are likewise].
And there are four types of *triṣṭubh*:
[the first] is "āgminendra yāhi" (RV 8.40), belonging to the hymn consisting of twenty-four verses.
Śyāvāśva Ātreya [composed] the *upariṣṭājyotis* for the Aśvins;
the twenty-second and twenty-fourth [verses] are *paṅkti*s, while the twenty-third consists of two *mahābṛhatī*s.
For the seventh [verse], "avitāsī," Śyāvāśva [addressed] Indra Śakra.
The last [verse] has Mahāpati as its deity; [the hymn] beginning with "agrimeṣṭhau" consists of ten verses; Nābhāka is the seer; and the last [verse] is a Paṅkti of Kaṇva.
"Ime viprasya" (RV 8.74): for this hymn of thirty-three verses by Sūta Virūpa Āṅgirasa, Agni is the deity and Gāyatrī is the meter.
"Samidhāgnim" (RV 8.44): for this hymn of thirty verses, Virūpa Āṅgirasa is the seer, Agni is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter.
"To Śrādyāya":
Indra; the Gāyatrī meter.

This hymn consists of forty-four verses. Triśoka Kāṇva is the seer. For eighteen verses, the deity is Vitatrāsya Āditya. The other five verses have Uṣas as the deity; they are in the Mahāpaṅkti meter and destroy suffering.
*Pratiti*. Five verses. *Pṛṣan*, *Kāṇva*, Aindra-Gāyatra, Āgneya, Saurī, another Paṅkti; *prokṣa*.
The twelfth [section] consists of the *pragāthas* addressed to Indra as lord;
there is a variant reading: "upati."
Vrata-khaṇḍa, Chapter 1: Hemādri.
The seventh, eighth, and ninth [lunar days] are destructive; one should avoid them on these [days].
The *Ṛc* of the twenty-one-fold hymn: "The fish, the intoxicating one, Agastya" (RV 10.68).
There are many sages who carry nets; the Ādityas are the deity for the tenth [verse].
The Kādamī [verse] is among the Dvādaśīs; Aditi is its deity; the Gāyatrī is its meter;
"yo rājā" is its [beginning]; and the Vāhata is its [melody].
The first [verse] is addressed to Puruhanman;
the second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh are addressed to Indra; the eighth is a Satobṛhatī; the thirteenth is an Uṣṇih;
the fourteenth is an Anuṣṭubh; and the fifteenth is a Purauṣṇih.
In this [sūkta], "tvam agne mahobhiḥ," there is a hymn of fifteen verses.
Sudīti Puramaudgava is the seer, or alternatively [one of] the others.

[The Vratacana, Chapter 1] Death is the deity of the four *sukīyāma* verses; Dhātṛ is the deity of the fifth; Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity of the next; the following have the Pitṛs as their deities; and those ending with *antvā* have Prajāpati as their deity. The meter is Triṣṭubh.

The eleventh [verse] is a *prastārapaṅkti*; the thirteenth is a *jagatī*; the fourteenth is an *anuṣṭubh*. The first [verse] consists of a single word per line (*ekapadā*) for the sake of honor; the second is an *anuṣṭubh*.

The ninth [verse] is Virāj; the others are Triṣṭubhs. Of the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with *pra devatrā*, Pulūṣa Kaṇva is the seer, and Āponaptṛ or Apāṃnapāt is the deity; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The hymn beginning with *prāvepā mā* consists of fourteen verses;
Mojavat or the Seers are the seers. In the seventh and ninth [verses], there is the Cāyā [metre].

Praise of agriculture; praise of the Dvādaśī [twelfth lunar day]; censure of the Śeṣāyana [sect]. The hymn beginning with "Amba-nam" consists of fourteen verses; Dhānākolūṣa is the seer, the Viśvedevas are the deities, and the metre is Jagatī, with the last two verses in Triṣṭubh. The hymn beginning with "Namaḥ mitrasya" consists of twelve verses; Sūrya is the deity and the metre is Anuṣṭubh. The hymn beginning with "Abhitapyaḥ" has Sūrya as the deity.

The *jagatī* consists of two *daṃsa* [verses] and the *triṣṭubh*. For the purpose of praising the sky, there is the *vasaprī* and the *agni-triṣṭubh*; the other deities are those designated by their characteristic marks (*liṅgoktā devatāḥ*). "Mā pragāma" (do not depart) is this group of six;
"bandhu-bandhu-bandhu vipra-bandhavaḥ" (O kinsmen, O wise kinsmen) is the *indra-gāyatrī*. "Yateyamam" (this which is yours)... [is the next].
The four seers beginning with Babhru are the authors of the *dādartha* hymn; the *yamādi* hymns have the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
"Idam" consists of twenty-seven verses. Nābhānediṣṭha, Māmateya, the Viśvedevas, and Bṛhaspati are the authors of the *pratyekādartha* hymn, which has the *triṣṭubh* meter. Bṛhaspati...

The seers are the night; Prajāpati is the heaven and the *udumbara* tree; Śaṃyu is the *bṛhatī* meter and Indra is the *anuṣṭubh*; the cow is the *āpya* verse, and the serpents are the *gāyatrī* in its prior and posterior forms;
"sumitriyā naḥ" is Prajāpati and the waters; "durmitriyān" is likewise; and the earth is the deity.

"Samāvavarti" (It turns back together)—for this [verse], Agni Abhirata is the deity; it is in the *gāyatrī* meter. The *anuṣṭubh* [meter] for "viramrinuṣṭup" and "aṃśunā" is entirely *anuṣṭubh*. For "siñcati pariṣicati," the *sūrya* and *indrīvā* are *anuṣṭubh*. For "dhānāvantaṃ," Viśvāmitra is the seer and *gāyatrī* is the meter. For "uhadindrāya nṛmedha pura—" [the seer is Nṛmedha].

"Medhasāt indro br̥hataḥ"—for this *nṛcakṣas* hymn, Madhucchandas is the seer, Sarasvatī is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter. "Śrāmandorvi khāmiva"—Indra is the deity for this *br̥hatī*. "Cāno viśāsu havyam"—Śyāvāśva is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the *br̥hatī* is the meter.

"Kamome rājan viti," O Brahman, is a *kāma* [verse] in the *triṣṭubh* meter;
"Bhadrāya kaḥ saṃcadravya" is by the two seers Kośika and Ākhi, in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
"Tubhyameva janimantviti" is by Śaṃyu; "Jarimā" is in the Triṣṭubh meter;
and "Āyātu mitra" [is the next].
*mitrāvaruṇāvāpo'gnayaḥ*: Triṣṭubh; *āśānāmāthāpālebhyaḥ*:
Vācaspati and the guardians of the quarters (*āśāpālāḥ*), Anuṣṭubh; *idañjanāso vidatha brahmā dyāvāpṛthivyau*: Anuṣṭubh; *agne gobhiḥ*: This [verse] belongs to Agni Brahmā.

*Triṣṭubh*. "The peaceful, the terrible..."—the son of [this hymn], Brahmā, Earth, Atmosphere, and Heaven—an *anuṣṭubh*. "Prayante yonir ṛtiyaḥ"—Atharvan, Agni—an *anuṣṭubh*. "Vividhānayā"—Atharvan, Agni—a *triṣṭubh*. "Bhravaṃdhu veṇa"—Atharvan, Soma.
*Anuṣṭubh*: "O King, [the plough] is yoked" (*adhuhe rājan*)—of these four verses, one is *triṣṭubh*.
"The two gods among the gods" (*yayor devauṣu*)—the *brahmā* priest recites this *anuṣṭubh* verse: "He yokes the ploughs, the yokes apart" (*yunakti sīrā viyugā*).
"Atharvan [yokes] the furrows" (*atharvā sītā*)—this is a *triṣṭubh*. "With good pasture" (*suyavasāt*)—Atharvan and the *brahmā* priest recite this *triṣṭubh*.
*yadāgraḥ*—the deity is Vāk; *ekavarcas*—Agni; *anuṣṭubh*. *Arhate bhagaḥ*—this [verse];
*Atharvā sītā*; *triṣṭubh*. *Ete panyāḥ panyām panyāḥ*—*atijagatī*. *Avitasta iti*; *Brahmā unmocanaḥ*; *paṅkti*. *Yo...*
"nasvī araṇī" is by Atharvan; the deity is Īśvara; the meter is Triṣṭubh. "grahavahaṃditi" consists of six [verses];
the deity is Indra; the meter is Triṣṭubh. "tvamuttamam" is here addressed to Soma; the meter is Anuṣṭubh.
"yathā yaśacandramasi" is addressed to Varuṇa and Candramas; the meter is Jagatī. "śranīśragni" [is addressed to] Agni.

*Pativedanaḥ somaḥ* is in the *triṣṭubh* meter; *yena devāḥ* is the *śrīyamapām arghyamā*, or according to others, the *anuṣṭubh*. *Yat pṛthivyām anāvṛttam* is a ritual formula (*kalpamantra*). I do not state the meters, seers, or deities. *Śivaḥ śivebhiḥ*—this [verse] has Brahmā as its seer and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Thus [ends the section].

The *dūṣaṇa* [rite] consists of the hymn *brahmakṛtyādūṣaṇam* in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; the verse *ihaiva sta māpa yāta* (or *ihaiva stana paripātu*) is addressed to Bṛhaspati in the *triṣṭubh* meter; and the hymn *mā no vidad abhiśastaye* is for the *brahmā*.
The deity of the [first] verse is Īśvara; the meter is Anuṣṭubh. The deity of "avāno agnir adhyakṣaḥ" is Agni; the seer is Kauśika; the meter is Anuṣṭubh.

For the three verses beginning with "pūṣāvitā," the deity is Śakra. The meter of the first is Paṅkti, that of the two following is Anuṣṭubh, and the others are Gāyatrī. These are the hymns beginning with "pragāṇaya."

The first three [verses] are generally in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; "devā māruta" and "brahmā madata" are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. "muccāmi tvā" is from the *sūta*, [addressed to] Yamanāthana; "indrāgnī" is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Now, the *Atharvaśiras*: "agnir" is ash, "vāyur" is breath.
"Water is ashes; the self is ashes; indeed, everything is ashes"—this is the injunction of the Atharvans.

The seers (ṛṣis) of the syllable *oṃ* are Indra and the Ṛṣis. According to the *Yājuṣa-sarvānukrama*, Brahmā is the seer of the supreme *praṇava*—the supreme Brahman which is the support for yogins, consisting of the syllable *om*, and endowed with qualities such as grossness (*sthūla*) and so forth; its metre is *gāyatrī*. It is the Supreme Self.

The deity is [the object] of application in all cases—whether at the commencement and conclusion of rituals, in sacrifices, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth; in rites for peace (*śānti*); in other various rites, whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and so on.
And thus says Bhāṭṭagāyana: "Giving, sacrifice, austerity, Vedic study, recitation, meditation, and the twilight prayers..."

In the *Pāraśara-prāṇāyāma-homa-devapitr-mantra-uccāraṇa-brahmārambha*, it is stated that one should maintain awareness of the *praṇavas*. In the *Mantrārtha-pravarttaka*, the necessity of knowing the seers (*ṛṣi*), deities (*devatā*), and meters (*chandas*) is declared. Furthermore, the nature of the seers, deities, and meters is described in the *Yājuṣa-sarvānukrama*.
If one studies, recites, mutters, offers oblations, sacrifices, or officiates at sacrifices without knowing these [sumas],
his Vedic knowledge does not long remain effective;
he goes to ruin, he is consumed by sin, or he becomes worse off— this is the delusion of those called Chandogas.

**Hemādri** [[page 490-to-490]] *Hemādri* (The Mountain of Gold) is a monumental compendium of Dharmaśāstra (Hindu law and religious duty) composed by the thirteenth-century scholar Hemādri. It is divided into five major sections (*khaṇḍas*): *Vratakhanda*, *Dānakhaṇḍa*, *Kālanirṇayakhaṇḍa*, *Mokṣakhaṇḍa*, and *Pariseṣakhaṇḍa*. This work is renowned for its vast collection of citations from ancient Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other authoritative sources, providing detailed prescriptions for religious observances, gifts, astrological calculations, liberation, and various supplementary topics. It remains a primary reference for understanding medieval Hindu ritual and legal traditions.

Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom does not perceive form as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive forms as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive eye-contact as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as having an intrinsic nature.

He does not perceive the earth element as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the faculty of faith as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the faculties of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the power of faith as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the powers of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the limb of awakening of mindfulness as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the limbs of awakening of investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the path as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the fruits of the ascetic life or nirvāṇa as having an intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom trains in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, gradually ascend through the stages of a bodhisattva? How does he enter the certainty of a bodhisattva? How does he fulfill the perfections? How does he fulfill the thirty-seven dharmas conducive to awakening? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, gradually ascends through the stages of a bodhisattva; he enters the certainty of a bodhisattva; he fulfills the perfections; he fulfills the thirty-seven dharmas conducive to awakening; he fulfills the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the unique buddha-dharmas, and the great compassion; he fulfills the marks and secondary characteristics of a great man; he purifies the Buddha-field; he matures beings; and he goes forth to the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, if emptiness of intrinsic nature were not a dharma, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. On a level, pure ground smeared with red sandalwood paste,

In this world, there is no medicine other than the Sun that cures disease and destroys illness—
for he who follows the path of the Sun is devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
From the mere sight of him, the destruction of disease occurs;
how indeed could there be the occurrence of disease or poverty for those devoted to the Sun?
O best of the Bharatas, when the Supreme Lord is directly perceived,
a person who observes the vow for seven months in succession becomes a practitioner of the vow.
A man devoted to the Sun, observing the fast and intent on the welfare of all beings,
should, accompanied by Brahmins on the eighth lunar day, feed them with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
He whose eleventh year and his seventh year are of divine form,
having pierced through the orb of the sun, goes to the eternal Brahman.

Sangha: The community of Buddhist practitioners; specifically, the order of monks and nuns. Sila: Moral virtue; ethical conduct. Sotapanna: A stream-enterer; one who has entered the stream leading to Nibbana and is guaranteed of full enlightenment. Tathagata: An epithet for a Buddha, meaning "One who has come thus" or "One who has gone thus. Upadana: Clinging or grasping; the attachment to sense-pleasures, views, rituals, and the doctrine of self. Vipassana: Insight meditation; the direct observation of the impermanent, suffering, and non-self nature of phenomena. Yama: The lord of the dead or the god of death; a deity associated with the underworld. Yoni: Womb or place of birth; the mode of rebirth (e.g., egg-born, womb-born). Abhidhamma: The third division of the Pali Canon, containing philosophical and psychological analyses of experience. Arahant: A person who has attained the highest level of spiritual development and is no longer subject to rebirth. Asava: Mental fermentations
